e.t: This word is a proper name, rendered “Abeddara” or “Aveththara.” It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament text, rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs seven times, in five verses across 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be identified more precisely here. Its repeated use is concentrated in the accounts recorded in 2 Samuel 6 and 1 Chronicles 13.

This word is an adverb meaning “very” or “much.” It strengthens the word or statement it modifies, showing an increased degree or intensity rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:11. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic function is to emphasize how strongly or greatly something is expressed.

This word means “blood” and can refer to blood as the life-bearing fluid within the body or to bloodstreams. It is a noun used throughout the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, appearing 386 times in this corpus. Its ordinary sense remains physical blood, including blood poured out, shed, or present in a living body. The surrounding passage determines its particular significance, but the word itself consistently identifies blood as a bodily substance.

This adjective means “indissoluble”: not able to be dissolved, broken apart, or brought to an end. It describes something viewed as firmly lasting rather than temporary or easily undone. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 10:11. Its exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is something that cannot be dissolved or separated.

Alemoi; Alemi is a proper name, identifying a named person, place, or group rather than expressing an action or quality. The available lexical wording preserves the name in these closely related forms, but does not specify which kind of named entity it identifies. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 5:26. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX noun means a “step” or “stair,” referring to something used for moving upward or downward. It names a physical feature rather than an action or abstract idea. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Exodus 20:26, so its normal meaning is defined by this straightforward sense rather than by a broad range of uses. The precise role it plays in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its translation context.

This Greek LXX verb means “break up.” It describes something being split, burst apart, or opened with force, rather than remaining whole and closed. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, all in 2 Kings. Because it is a verb, it expresses an action—what someone or something does. Its precise force in any one verse depends on what is being broken up and the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains forceful separation or opening.

This Greek LXX verb means to put up with something or to bear up under it. It describes continuing to endure a person, situation, or burden rather than giving way immediately. The word appears 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, so it expresses a recurring idea of patient endurance. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central sense remains steadfastly bearing what is difficult or unwelcome.

This noun means “hatred”: a deep and settled aversion toward someone or something. It names the feeling itself rather than an action, command, or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:1. The surrounding verse is needed to show whose hatred is meant and how the word functions there. Its basic sense describes an inward disposition of hostility rather than a brief disagreement or passing dislike.

This verb means “reveal” or “uncover”: it describes making something hidden or covered become visible or known. It can refer to bringing something into view, exposing what was concealed, or making information available. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 85 times, showing regular use across different kinds of passages. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being revealed or uncovered there.

This verb means “finish off,” describing the act of bringing something to its completion or end. It expresses completion rather than merely beginning or continuing an action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 15:39. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is to complete, conclude, or finish something.

This noun means “one who does”—a person identified by carrying out an action or undertaking something. It presents the person as the doer rather than describing the action itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 12:6. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the particular action or role intended in that passage must be understood from its context.

gl: separate offering; that which is set apart
d: separate offering; that which is set apart

e.t: This noun means a separate offering—something set apart for a distinct purpose. It refers to an item or portion distinguished from what is ordinary, especially in passages concerning offerings and sacred portions. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times across 10 verses, from Exodus through Ezekiel. The central idea is separation: something is marked off and dedicated rather than treated as common. Its exact reference in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

“Baalimath” or “Vaalimath” is a proper name, used to identify a specific named person or place in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general description or action word, so its meaning is primarily the name itself rather than an idea translated into English. This word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 5:16. The surrounding verse text would be needed to determine exactly whom or what the name identifies there.

Barsa, also rendered Varsa, is a proper name rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a named referent instead of expressing a general concept. The name occurs once, in Genesis 14:2. Its precise referent cannot be determined from the name alone, but must be understood from the surrounding passage. This is a Greek LXX name and should not be treated as a general vocabulary term.

This adjective means "for the council," describing something connected with or intended for a council. It identifies a council-related function rather than naming the council itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 24:6. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s specific force in that passage must be understood from its sentence and context.

Gadeōni is a proper name, referring to a person named Gadeoni, also rendered Gatheoni. It functions as a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in Numbers, from Numbers 1:11 through Numbers 10:24. The name appears in lists and records identifying this individual. Its exact significance beyond identifying the person is not stated by the available biblical wording.

This word means “treasurer,” a person responsible for keeping or administering a treasury. It is a noun naming an official rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 28:1, so its normal meaning is clear even though the supplied verse text does not provide additional context. The word points to a recognized responsibility involving valuable resources or funds.

This adverb describes doing something nobly or bravely—with courage, dignity, and honorable purpose. It tells how an action is carried out rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 11 times, all in the deuterocanonical books, especially 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains conduct marked by courage and nobility.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Dadan” and also identified as “Thathan.” It functions as a name rather than as a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 10:7. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, it does not establish whether the name refers to a person, a place, or another named entity. Its basic meaning is therefore the proper name itself: Dadan, also called Thathan.

This word means “reconcile”: to restore agreement between parties who are divided or at odds. It is a verb, so it describes the act of bringing about peace or renewed harmony rather than merely naming a peaceful condition. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs eight times, appearing in passages from 1 Samuel, Job, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any one verse depends on who is being reconciled and what caused the division, but its central idea remains the restoration of a broken relationship.

This noun means “double cloak,” referring to a garment understood as a cloak with a doubled or layered covering. It names a type of clothing rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, the word occurs nine times, showing that it is used for this specific garment across several books. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes someone or something infamous or shameful—marked by disgrace rather than honor. It can identify a person, action, or condition that deserves a bad reputation or brings shame. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 3 Maccabees, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included. The word’s precise force in either passage depends on what or whom it describes.

This verb means “abhor” or “detest”: it expresses a strong rejection of something regarded as deeply offensive or hateful. As a verb, it describes the act of feeling or showing intense aversion rather than simple dislike. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Proverbs 8:7. Its precise force in that verse is best understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to powerful revulsion and rejection.

This Greek LXX verb means “reap”: to gather a crop after it has grown. It describes the act of harvesting what has been planted or allowed to mature. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, all in Leviticus, across two verses. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming the crop, field, or person involved. The surrounding verse determines whether it refers to ordinary agricultural work or to a specific instruction about harvesting. Its basic meaning remains the act of reaping or gathering a crop.

This noun refers to “sobering up; rest”—a return to clear-mindedness or a condition of relief and repose. It presents rest not merely as inactivity, but as a settling or recovery after disturbance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Lamentations. Its exact emphasis may lean toward renewed composure or quiet rest according to the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is recovery into calmness and steadiness.

This verb means “conceive”—to become pregnant or begin carrying a child. It describes the beginning of pregnancy rather than the later stages of bearing or giving birth. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 5:28. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself plainly refers to conception. The rendering “conceive” directly expresses its ordinary meaning as an action or event.

Eliezer is a personal name used for people in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than a general description, title, action, or quality. The name appears 14 times in 13 verses in this Greek Old Testament corpus, from Genesis 15:2 through Ezra 10:31. Its occurrences include Genesis 15:2, Exodus 18:4, and several genealogical or historical passages in Chronicles. The name itself identifies a person; the surrounding verse is needed to determine which Eliezer is meant in a particular passage.

Elphal, also rendered Elfal, is a proper name identifying a person rather than a general idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 11:35. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide a further meaning or explanation of its name components. Its role is therefore to distinguish this individual within the biblical record.

This Greek LXX verb means “belittle,” describing speech or action that treats someone as insignificant or unworthy of respect. In the Septuagint corpus, it occurs 23 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding wording and situation, but its central idea is lowering another person rather than honoring them, whether through speech, conduct, or contemptuous treatment.

This word means “arcade,” a covered architectural passage or gallery. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament text of Ezekiel to identify parts of the temple’s planned structure. The word occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, all within Ezekiel, especially in the temple vision described across chapters 40–46. Its repeated use reflects a specific architectural feature rather than an action, quality, or person. The exact arrangement or purpose of each arcade must be understood from the surrounding passage.

This LXX word means “commander,” referring to a person who holds authority over others. Used as a noun or adjective, it identifies someone connected with leadership or command rather than an ordinary private person. It occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX material, including passages in Ezra, Nehemiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is a recognized leader or commanding official.

This word means “ordinance”: an officially established command, rule, or decree. As a noun, it refers to something laid down with authority and intended to direct or govern conduct. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, including passages in Daniel, Wisdom, 3 Maccabees, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains an authoritative ordinance or decree.

This Greek LXX noun means “dispute” or “rivalry”: a condition of contention, opposition, or competing with others. It describes conflict between people rather than peaceful agreement. In the Greek text of Sirach, it occurs three times, at Sirach 28:11, 40:4, and 40:9. The surrounding wording determines whether the emphasis falls on an argument, ongoing contention, or competitive opposition, but the central idea remains hostile disagreement or rivalry.

This adjective means “changeable,” describing someone or something that can shift from one state, condition, or course to another. It points to a lack of steadiness rather than naming a particular action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 17:20. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what is being described there, but the word itself presents the idea of changeability or inconsistency. Its meaning is therefore simple and direct: not fixed, constant, or settled.

This noun refers to something characterized by “ready use”—being prepared or available for use. It names the quality or condition of being ready for use rather than describing an action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, in 3 Maccabees 2:33. The precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning is the state of ready use.

This verb means “lead” or “consider.” It can describe guiding people or directing them, and it can also express regarding something in a particular way or taking it into account. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 140 times across 138 verses, showing that it is used for both leadership and thoughtful judgment. Its exact sense in a particular verse depends on whether the sentence focuses on directing others or evaluating something.

This Greek LXX noun refers to pleasant living marked by comfort, enjoyment, or luxury. It describes a lifestyle centered on ease and material satisfaction rather than hardship or simplicity. The word appears twice in the Greek text of 4 Maccabees, in 4 Maccabees 2:2 and 2:4. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense remains the enjoyment of comfortable, luxurious living.

This word means “whenever” or “when”. It is an adverb that marks the time something happens, linking an action or event with a particular occasion. Depending on the sentence, it can point to a specific time or to any time that a stated condition occurs. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 96 times, so it serves as a regular way to introduce or identify timing rather than expressing an action, person, or object. Its exact force in a verse comes from the surrounding words and sentence. [p03:word:lxx:L706008:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L706008:occurrences]

Tharra is a proper name, functioning as a specific personal or place designation rather than as a general description or action. The available lexical definition gives only the name itself, so its exact referent must be identified from the surrounding passage rather than from the word alone. In the Greek Old Testament data, Tharra occurs twice, both times in Esther 1. [Could be a name or title?]

This Greek LXX noun means “meal” or “feast,” referring to food prepared and eaten as a gathering or occasion. It can describe an ordinary meal or a celebratory feast, depending on the surrounding passage. The word occurs twice in the LXX corpus, in Wisdom and 3 Maccabees. Its basic sense is a shared eating occasion rather than a person, action, or abstract quality.

Jabin is a personal name, rendered “Jabin” or “Iabin.” It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament, rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. The name occurs nine times across eight verses, appearing especially in Judges and also in Joshua, 1 Samuel, and Psalms. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding text and the person being named there.

Iarim is a proper name, referring to a named person or place rather than expressing a general quality, action, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times across seven verses, appearing in Joshua, 1 Chronicles, and Hosea. The supplied lexical meaning identifies it simply as “Iarim”; the surrounding verse is needed to determine whether a particular occurrence names a person, location, or another proper designation. It should therefore be read as a name whose precise reference comes from its immediate context.

Iiēl, also rendered Iil, is a proper name used to identify a person. It is not a word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is primarily the individual whom the name identifies in each passage. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 28 times across 25 verses, chiefly in 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, and Ezra. The particular person identified must be determined from the surrounding passage.

“Isabia” or “Isavia” is a personal name, not a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 4:35. Since the available text does not provide a wider definition or surrounding context, its meaning is limited to identifying the person who bears this name. The two forms are approved renderings of the same name in this LXX entry.

Iōdan, also written Iothan, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 2 Chronicles 29:12. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, no further personal details or contextual significance can be stated reliably from the name alone.

This Greek LXX noun means a “pitcher,” referring to a vessel used for holding or pouring liquid. It appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 4 Maccabees 3:12. The lexical sense itself is straightforward: the word names an object, not an action, quality, or person. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here.

Karmēlios is a proper name, given in English as “Karmēlios” or “Karmilios.” It functions as a distinctive name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times across nine verses, from 1 Samuel 25:4 through 2 Kings 4:25. The references show repeated use of this name, while the available lexical information does not provide a broader descriptive meaning or explain the identity named in each passage.

Katasem is a proper name, rendered simply as “Katasem,” rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 19:13. The name itself does not identify whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise referent must therefore be learned from the surrounding passage, not from the name alone.

This Greek LXX verb means “dare” or “presume.” It describes a person taking bold action or venturing to act, with “presume” highlighting the possibility of acting too boldly or confidently. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX text, both in 2 Maccabees, at 2 Maccabees 3:24 and 5:15. These references identify its occurrences, while the surrounding verse text is needed to determine the precise force in each setting.

This Greek LXX verb means “adorn” or “trim”: to make something more attractive, orderly, or fitting by arranging or decorating it. It can describe beautifying an object, a person, or something prepared for proper appearance. The word occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, so its basic sense is used across several settings rather than being limited to one kind of decoration. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being adorned or trimmed.

This is a proper name, rendered “Laphidōth” or “Lafithoth,” identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it appears only once, at Judges 4:4. The available lexical information establishes the name’s identity and spelling, but does not provide a separate descriptive meaning or word-picture. Its precise significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage, not from this name alone.

Maalon is a proper name—the Greek LXX rendering of a man named Maalon. It identifies the same person wherever it appears, rather than describing an object, action, or quality. The name occurs four times in the LXX, all in the book of Ruth: Ruth 1:2, Ruth 1:5, Ruth 4:9, and Ruth 4:10. Because the available word-level information does not include the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes identity, while the passages supply the details about the person and his place in the narrative.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Mathanai” or “Mathane.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 10:37. Because it is a personal name, its basic meaning is the individual it names; the name itself does not provide a broader definition or spiritual concept. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person’s place in the list.

gl: great of flesh; with a great member
d: great of flesh; with a great member

e.t: This adjective describes someone or something as “great of flesh; with a great member,” referring to notable physical size. It is a bodily description rather than a general statement about greatness, strength, or importance. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, in Ezekiel 16:26. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, its precise force in that occurrence cannot be explained beyond this basic physical meaning. Its single occurrence makes it an uncommon word in the Greek Old Testament.

μερισμός means “apportioning” or “allocation”: the act of dividing something and assigning each portion or share. As a noun, it names the distribution itself rather than the person who distributes or the thing being divided. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice, in Joshua 11:23 and Ezra 6:18. Its basic sense therefore concerns an ordered sharing or assignment, while the surrounding verse determines what is being apportioned and how that distribution functions in the passage.

This noun refers to a body part located behind the midriff—the middle area of the torso. Its meaning is physical and anatomical rather than describing a person, action, or spiritual quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in Deuteronomy, Psalms, and Isaiah. The word identifies a specific region of the body, while the surrounding verse determines how that body part functions in each passage.

This word means “not.” It is used in the Greek Old Testament to express negation, denying or prohibiting something in a statement. As a conjunction or adverb, it functions as a small but important word that can reject an action, description, or expectation. It appears 2,897 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing that negation is a frequent part of biblical speech and instruction. Its exact force in any sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central meaning remains “not.”

This noun means “uncleanness”: a condition or quality of being unclean. It names uncleanness as a concept rather than describing an action by itself. In the Greek Septuagint tradition represented here, it occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees 6, at verses 19 and 25. Those references identify its limited recorded range in this corpus, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the specific situation in each occurrence.

Naath is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 6:11. The available meaning is simply the name “Naath”; the name itself does not provide further information about the person’s character, role, or significance. Understanding those details would require the surrounding verse and genealogical context, rather than the name alone.

This word means “spun,” describing material that has been made into thread by twisting fibers. It functions as an adjective, identifying something by the way it was prepared rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Exodus 31:4. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the thing it describes.

This Greek LXX noun means a “bough” or “branch”—a woody part growing from a tree or similar plant. It refers to a physical part of vegetation rather than an action or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 13:13. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here, but its ordinary meaning remains a branch or bough of a plant.

gl: having an equal right to vote with
d: having an equal right to vote with

e.t: This adjective describes someone who has "having an equal right to vote with" another person or group. It expresses shared voting standing: the person is counted as an equal participant in a decision. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:20, but the surrounding verse text is not available here, so the particular situation must be understood from its context.

“Ophar” or “Ofar” is a proper name, used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) text rather than to express an idea, action, or quality. The name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 11:36. Since no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, its personal identity and significance in that passage must be understood from the passage itself, not from the name alone.

This noun means “parable,” referring to an illustrative saying or story that communicates meaning through a comparison or pictured expression. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 44 times, including passages in Numbers, Psalms, Ezekiel, and Sirach. The word identifies the parable itself as a form of expression. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic lexical sense remains “parable.”

This word means “fifteen,” naming the quantity that comes after fourteen and before sixteen. It functions as an indeclinable number, so it identifies a count or amount rather than describing an action, person, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times across seven verses, including passages involving measurements, valuations, provisions, and an amount of money. Its basic meaning remains numerical; the surrounding passage determines what is being counted or measured.

This Greek LXX verb means “drenched; sunk in.” It describes being thoroughly soaked or immersed, emphasizing a condition of being overwhelmed by liquid rather than merely touched by it. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 15:32. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains the experience of being saturated or submerged.

This verb means to scalp someone in the Scythian way—that is, to remove the scalp as a form of violent bodily harm. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 7:4. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the exact force of the action in that passage, but the word itself plainly refers to this brutal act.

This noun means “brick-making”: the work or activity of producing bricks. It refers to making bricks, not to the bricks themselves. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Exodus 5:7. Because the word is attested in only that single location, its basic meaning is clear, while its precise force in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX adjective means “how much?” It is used to ask about quantity or amount, directing attention to the size or extent of something rather than naming the thing itself. In a sentence, it functions as an interrogative describing the amount being asked about. The word appears 11 times in this Greek LXX corpus, in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding question.

This Greek LXX verb means “choose” or “decide.” It describes an act of making a deliberate choice rather than merely considering an option. As a verb, it presents choosing or deciding as something a person does. In the LXX, it occurs twice, both in 3 Maccabees, so its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context. Its central idea remains the exercise of personal decision: selecting one course, purpose, or response over another.

This verb means to foretell—to announce or make known something before it happens. It describes speaking beforehand about a future matter, rather than merely reporting what is already known. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 41:26. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains the act of declaring something in advance.

This verb means to perceive something additionally—to become aware of something alongside what is already being perceived. It describes an added act of awareness rather than perception in general. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times in five verses, appearing in Numbers, Judges, Job, and Isaiah. Its precise force in any verse depends on what the surrounding sentence presents as the additional thing perceived.

“Captain” means a person who holds command and directs others. In the Greek Old Testament, this noun identifies a leader by position rather than an action or quality. Its basic meaning is focused and specific: someone responsible for command and direction. The word occurs twice in the LXX, showing a limited but consistent use. The surrounding verse identifies precisely whom this title describes in each occurrence, while the word itself presents that person as a captain or commander.

This word means “pieces of wood.” It is a noun for wooden pieces mentioned as material or objects in biblical descriptions. The term occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, so it refers to a recognizable physical item rather than an abstract idea. Its exact role—such as what the pieces were used for—depends on the surrounding verse, but the basic meaning remains pieces of wood.

Rathama is a proper name, rendered “Rathama” in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a specific name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in Numbers 33:18–19. The available information identifies the name and its occurrences, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whether Rathama refers to a place, person, or another named entity.

Regma, also rendered Rhegma, is a proper name rather than an ordinary descriptive word. It functions as a specific name in the Greek Old Testament, so its meaning is primarily the identity of the person, place, or name being mentioned in each passage, not a general quality or action. It occurs five times across three verses, in Genesis, Joshua, and 1 Chronicles. The exact referent in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Sanaa is a proper name, rendered simply as “Sanaa.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs three times: once in 1 Chronicles 9:7, once in Ezra 2:35, and once in Nehemiah 7:38. The exact person, family, or place identified by the name must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage.

Sedem, also rendered Sethem, is a proper name. It identifies a particular named person or place in the Greek Old Testament, but the available information does not establish which kind of referent it names. This word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Ezra 10:43. Its precise significance there must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage rather than from the name itself.

This Greek LXX noun means “decay” or “putrefaction,” referring to the process or condition in which something decomposes. It names physical deterioration rather than an action of repairing or preserving. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Isaiah 14:11, so its precise force there must be understood from that passage’s surrounding words. Its basic sense remains the breakdown and rotting of something that has lost its former condition.

This Greek LXX noun means “covering; shelter.” It refers to something that covers, protects, or provides refuge, whether a physical covering or a place of shelter. The word appears 19 times in the LXX corpus represented here, including passages rendered with “shelter” and “covering.” Its basic sense therefore centers on being covered or having a place of protection. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on the covering itself or the refuge it provides.

This noun means “anything that encircles”—something arranged around another object or area. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for surrounding or enclosing parts of objects and structures, including details connected with the furnishings described in Exodus. The word occurs eight times in this corpus, across seven verses, with most occurrences in Exodus. Its precise reference in any passage depends on the object or structure being described there.

This Greek LXX verb means “spread” or “make a bed.” It describes laying something out, especially preparing a place for lying down or resting. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament represented by the LXX data, appearing in Esther, Job, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its basic sense remains practical: arranging or spreading out a bed or bedding, though the surrounding passage determines the particular object being prepared or laid out.

e.t: This word means “it must be conceded” or “it must be allowed.” It expresses something that ought to be admitted, accepted, or granted as necessary. As an adjective, it describes what must be acknowledged rather than presenting a personal preference or optional choice. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 2:31. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense is a required concession or permission.

This noun refers to anything agreed upon in advance, especially a preconcerted signal used for recognition or coordinated action. It names something whose meaning depends on prior agreement between people, rather than an ordinary object understood in the same way by everyone. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines exactly what agreed signal or arrangement is meant in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX verb means “feed together,” describing people or living beings sharing nourishment or being brought up together. It presents feeding as a joint activity rather than something done separately. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Daniel, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea is shared feeding or common upbringing.

Tanachi, also rendered Tanakhi, is a proper name referring to a particular person rather than describing an action or quality. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Numbers 26:39. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific family or narrative setting cannot be described further. Its central meaning is therefore its identifying function: Tanachi is the personal name of an individual mentioned in that passage.

This verb means “tormented” or “vexed,” describing the experience of being troubled, distressed, or harassed. It presents suffering or inner disturbance rather than a neutral feeling. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in the book of Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central sense is clear: someone is being troubled or made to suffer.

This noun refers to an apparition or phantom—a seeming appearance rather than an ordinary person or object. It is used four times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in Numbers, Job, Isaiah, and Wisdom. The word’s central idea remains the same across these occurrences: an apparition or phantom. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the appearance is being described.

“Wane” means to grow less or lose strength gradually. It is a verb describing something that diminishes rather than remaining full or strong. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Job 31:26. The lexical sense is clear even though no English rendering or surrounding verse text is available here. Its precise force in that passage depends on the sentence and context in which the verb appears.

This word means a fence or fencing—something built to enclose, mark off, or protect an area. It is a noun describing a physical barrier or boundary rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 19 times across 18 verses, chiefly in the Old Testament portion of the Greek Scriptures, and is also rendered “fence.” Its references range from Genesis through Sirach, showing use for boundaries and enclosed places. The exact sense in any particular verse is clarified by the surrounding passage.

This verb means “tumultuous,” describing action or behavior marked by turmoil rather than calm. As a verb, it portrays someone or something acting in a stirred-up, disorderly way, not simply existing in a troubled condition. The word therefore focuses on active disturbance. In the LXX, it occurs once, in Psalm 2:1. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly how that tumult is expressed there.

This proper name refers to “Chanaanitis” or “Khanaanitis,” the designation preserved in the Greek Septuagint. It is not presented here as a general action or quality, but as a named person or designation. The word occurs twice in the LXX corpus, once in 1 Chronicles 2:3 and once in Zechariah 11:7. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine its specific referent in each passage.

This noun means a string, specifically a gut-string. It names a physical cord rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, appearing once in Psalms and once in Nahum. Its basic sense is therefore a tangible string, while the precise way it functions in either verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage. The word’s explicit meaning is “gut-string; string.”

This noun means “winning of souls; persuasion.” It describes the act of persuading or drawing people, with emphasis on gaining them through influence rather than force. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 2:25. The word’s exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its argument, but its basic sense points to successfully persuading people or winning them over. It should therefore be understood as a term for persuasive influence directed toward people.

Ōbōth, also rendered Ovoth, is a proper name for a place. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, all in the book of Numbers, where the name identifies a location in Israel’s wilderness journey record. The word itself functions as a place-name rather than describing an action, quality, or person. Its exact significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its lexical sense is simply the named location Ōbōth.
